"The Unfinished Promise"

A Speech Advocating for Expanding the Rights of Undocumented Immigrants

Friends, neighbors, fellow believers in the American ideal—

I want to begin with a simple truth that should not be controversial: every person standing on this soil is a human being deserving of dignity. Not some people. Not documented people. Not people who arrived through the right channels at the right time with the right resources. Every person.

And yet today, roughly eleven million people who live among us—who build our homes, harvest our food, care for our children and our elderly, pay billions in taxes, and breathe the same air as every one of us—exist in a shadow. A shadow we created. A shadow we maintain. And a shadow we have the power—and I would argue the moral obligation—to lift.

I'm here to make the case that expanding the rights of undocumented immigrants isn't just compassionate policy. It is smart policy. It is just policy. And it is policy that reflects who we say we are when we put our hand over our heart and talk about liberty and justice for all.

I. The Moral Foundation

Let me start where I believe all good policy must start—with principle.

This nation was founded on a radical declaration: that certain rights are not granted by governments. They are inherent. Life. Liberty. The pursuit of happiness. The founders didn't write "for citizens only." They wrote that these truths are self-evident for all people. That language was intentional. It was aspirational. And for two and a half centuries, the story of America has been the slow, painful, beautiful work of living up to that aspiration—extending the circle of who counts as fully human in the eyes of the law.

We extended it to people who were enslaved. We extended it to women. We extended it to those without property, to people of every race, to people with disabilities. Every single time, there were voices that said, "Not them. Not yet. They haven't earned it." And every single time, history proved those voices wrong.

Today, those same voices say it about undocumented immigrants. And I am here to tell you: history will prove them wrong again.

Because the question before us is not a bureaucratic question about paperwork and visa categories. It is a moral question. Do we believe that a mother who crossed a desert to save her child's life deserves to see a doctor without fear of deportation? Do we believe that a teenager who has known no other home but this one deserves an education and a future? Do we believe that a man who has paid taxes, followed the law, and contributed to his community for twenty years deserves a voice in the local decisions that affect his daily life?

I believe the answer is yes. And I believe most of you, in your hearts, believe it too.

II. Access to Essential Public Services

Let me be specific about what I'm advocating, because vagueness is the enemy of progress.

First: every undocumented person in this country should have access to essential public services—healthcare, education, emergency assistance, and legal protection—without fear.

This is not radical. This is practical.

Right now, we have millions of people who avoid emergency rooms until a treatable condition becomes a life-threatening crisis—which we then pay for at ten times the cost. We have parents who won't report crimes because they're terrified that calling the police will lead to a deportation van. We have children who go hungry because their families are afraid to access nutrition programs. We have workers who are exploited, underpaid, and abused because they have no legal recourse, which drives down wages and working conditions for everyone.

This is not a system that protects American citizens. This is a system that hurts all of us.

When undocumented residents can access preventive healthcare, our emergency rooms are less overwhelmed, communicable diseases are better controlled, and our communities are healthier. When they can report crimes without fear, our neighborhoods are safer—for everyone. When their children are educated, our workforce is stronger and our economy grows.

Every credible economic analysis tells us the same story: inclusion is not a drain on resources. Exclusion is. Fear is expensive. Shadows are expensive. A permanent underclass with no access to basic services is a burden on every system we have.

But let me be clear—even if the economics didn't work out, even if there were no fiscal argument to be made, I would still stand here and make this case. Because we do not condition human dignity on a cost-benefit analysis. We do not tell a sick child, "I'm sorry, but treating you isn't in the budget." Not in this country. Not if we mean what we say.

III. The Case for Local Voting Rights

Now let me address the issue I know makes some of you uncomfortable. Local voting rights.

Take a breath. Stay with me.

I am not talking about federal elections. I am talking about school boards. City councils. Municipal ballot measures. The hyper-local decisions that determine whether a pothole gets fixed, whether a school gets funded, whether a zoning change transforms or destroys a neighborhood.

Here is the principle: the people affected by government decisions should have a say in those decisions. That is not a progressive principle or a conservative principle. It is a democratic principle. It is the very principle on which this nation was born—remember "no taxation without representation"?

Undocumented immigrants pay sales taxes every time they buy groceries. They pay property taxes—directly or through rent. Many pay income taxes and Social Security taxes using Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers, contributing to a system from which they will never collect benefits. By some estimates, undocumented immigrants contribute over $11 billion in state and local taxes every single year.

They pay taxes. They send their children to local schools. They use local roads, drink local water, depend on local fire departments. They are affected by every decision a city council makes. And yet they have zero voice. Zero representation. Zero power.

We fought a revolution over this principle. And now we look the other way when it applies to people we'd rather not see.

This is not without precedent. Non-citizen voting in local elections was common in the United States for most of its history. More than forty states allowed it at various points. Several municipalities—including places in Maryland and Vermont—permit it today. The republic has not crumbled. Democracy has not collapsed. What has happened is that communities have become more engaged, more representative, and more responsive to the people who actually live in them.

Giving people a stake in their community doesn't weaken democracy. It strengthens it. It brings people out of the shadows and into the civic fabric. It says: you matter here. You belong here. And because you belong, you have a responsibility—and a right—to participate.

IV. Confronting the Objections

Now, I know the objections. I have heard them. I take them seriously. Let me address them honestly.

"They broke the law."

Many did cross a border without authorization or overstayed a visa. I don't deny that. But let me ask you this: Is the appropriate punishment for a civil immigration violation—roughly equivalent to a traffic offense under federal law—a lifetime of fear, exploitation, and exclusion from basic human services? Is that proportional? Is that just?

And let's be honest about why people come here without documentation. They come because our legal immigration system is broken beyond recognition. Visa backlogs stretch for decades. A low-skilled worker from Mexico who applies through legal channels today may wait twenty years or more. If your child is starving, if gangs are threatening your family, if there is no future where you are—you do not wait twenty years. You do what any one of us would do. You move. You survive. You protect the people you love.

To punish people for navigating an impossible system while refusing to fix that system is not law and order. It is cruelty dressed up as principle.

"It's not fair to people who came legally."

I hear this, and I honor the sacrifice and patience of every person who navigated the legal immigration process. That process should be faster, fairer, and more accessible. Advocating for the undocumented does not diminish those who came through legal channels—it acknowledges that the system itself is failing everyone.

"We can't afford it."

We can't afford not to. As I've mentioned, the economic evidence consistently shows that integrating undocumented populations into public systems reduces costs, increases tax revenue, boosts economic productivity, and creates healthier and safer communities. The Congressional Budget Office, the National Academy of Sciences, and countless economists have confirmed this. Exclusion is the expensive choice.

"This will encourage more illegal immigration."

Providing basic services and local civic participation to people who are already here, who have been here for years or decades, is not an open border policy. It is a recognition of reality. Comprehensive immigration reform—which includes border policy, visa reform, and a pathway for those already here—is the answer to this concern. But we cannot hold eleven million people hostage to a comprehensive deal that Congress has failed to deliver for thirty years.

V. The Human Reality

I want to close with something that gets lost in policy debates: the human reality.

I'm talking about Maria, who has cleaned office buildings in this city for fifteen years, who has never missed a day of work, whose two children are American citizens and honor roll students—and who lives every single day with a knot of terror in her stomach because a traffic stop could separate her from her kids.

I'm talking about David, who was brought here at age three, who has never known another country, who graduated from high school with honors, who wants to serve his community—and who cannot legally drive to a job interview.

I'm talking about the elderly man in your neighborhood who shovels your sidewalk in winter and whose name you might not even know, who has a chronic condition he won't treat because he's afraid of the hospital, and who may die of something entirely preventable because we decided his humanity was conditional on a piece of paper.

These are not abstractions. These are your neighbors. They are woven into the fabric of your daily life in ways you may not even realize. And they are living in fear—not because they are dangerous, but because we have chosen to make their existence dangerous.

That is a choice. And we can make a different one.

VI. The Call

So here is what I am asking:

I am asking for the courage to see people as they are—not as political talking points, not as problems to be solved, but as human beings with the same hopes, fears, and aspirations that live in every one of our hearts.

I am asking for policies that reflect our values: access to healthcare, because no one should die from a treatable illness in the richest country on earth. Access to education, because an informed population benefits everyone. Protection under the law, because justice that excludes entire communities is not justice at all. And yes—a voice in local democracy, because people who contribute to a community deserve to help shape it.

I am asking you to reject the politics of fear and scarcity. There is not a finite amount of dignity in this country. Extending rights to others does not diminish your own. This is not a zero-sum game. A rising tide of inclusion lifts every single one of us.

And I am asking you to remember that throughout American history, every expansion of rights—every single one—was opposed by people who said it would destroy the nation. They said it about abolition. They said it about women's suffrage. They said it about civil rights. They said it about marriage equality. They were wrong then. And those who say it about immigrant rights are wrong now.

The arc of this nation's history bends—sometimes slowly, sometimes painfully—toward a wider embrace. Toward a more complete version of that founding promise. Toward a country that does not merely tolerate diversity but is strengthened by it.

Eleven million people are waiting—not for charity, not for pity, but for recognition of their humanity. For the chance to step out of the shadows and fully participate in the communities they already call home.

Let us be the generation that answers. Let us be the generation that chooses courage over fear, inclusion over exclusion, and dignity over indifference.

Let us, at long last, mean it when we say: liberty and justice for all.

Thank you.

Undocumented immigrants are not abstract statistics; they are parents, workers, and community members whose basic rights are routinely violated under current policies. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948 and endorsed by the United States, asserts in Article 25 that everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, including access to medical care, food, and social services.
